title: Take-home Exercise 1
text:
Insurance providers often face under-performing portfolios, driven by unclear causes of poor profitability and high market volatility. This project explores how visual analytics can help uncover hidden loss drivers, risk patterns and segmentation opportunities, and improved underwriting strategies.
Using a dataset from Mendeley Data, this analysis focuses on numerical, categorical, and temporal variables through univariate (one variable) and bivariate (two variables) analyses.
Empty data cells are ignored based on the Missing Completely at Random (MCAR) mechanism, as all variables can be considered completely independent of any observed values.




Gain deeper insights into portfolio performance and identify key factors affecting profitability and volatility in our portfolios.

title: Take-home Exercise 1
text:
Getting Started

Load Packages
We load the following R packages using the pacman::p_load() function:

tidyverse: Core collection of R packages designed for data science
treemapify: For creating treemap visualisations with ggplot2
colorspace: For perceptually-based colour palettes
hrbrthemes: Additional ggplot2 themes and typography
ggdist: For visualisations of distributions and uncertainty
ggstatsplot: For ggplot2-based plots with statistical annotations
plotly: For interactive web-based visualisations
corrplot: For visualising correlation matrices
ggrepel: For non-overlapping text labels in ggplot2
dplyr / ggplot2 / forcats / scales: Core data wrangling and visualisation utilities


pacman::p_load(
  tidyverse,
  treemapify,
  colorspace,
  hrbrthemes,
  ggdist,
  ggstatsplot,
  plotly,
  corrplot,
  dplyr,
  ggplot2,
  forcats,
  scales,
  ggrepel
)



Import Data
The dataset used is a motor insurance portfolio dataset retrieved from Mendeley Data. It is a semicolon-delimited CSV file and is imported as follows:

df <- read_delim("Dataset of motor insurance portfolio.csv",
                 delim = ";",
                 locale = locale(decimal_mark = "."),
                 show_col_types = FALSE)



Data Pre-processing

Variable Type Conversion and Derived Metrics
Several variables are coerced to their appropriate types (factors and numerics). Three important derived metrics are also computed:



Derived Metric
Formula




Loss Ratio
Total Incurred Losses / Total Premium


Claim Frequency
Total Claims / Total Exposure


Claim Severity
Total Incurred / Total Claims



Additionally, rows with missing values in key fields (vehicle_age, age_driving_licence, fuel_type, vehicle_value) are dropped, and records with invalid driver age (< 18) or negative vehicle age are filtered out.

clean_df <- df %>%
  drop_na(vehicle_age, age_driving_licence, fuel_type, vehicle_value) %>%

  mutate(
    policy_type        = as.factor(policy_type),
    policy_status      = as.factor(policy_status),
    business_type      = as.factor(business_type),
    payment_frequency  = as.factor(payment_frequency),
    bonus_score        = as.factor(bonus_score),
    fuel_type          = as.factor(fuel_type),
    vehicle_brand      = as.factor(vehicle_brand),
    municipality_type  = as.factor(municipality_type),
    circulation_area   = as.factor(circulation_area),
    year               = as.factor(year),

    total_exposure  = as.numeric(total_exposure),
    total_claims    = as.numeric(total_claims),
    total_premium   = as.numeric(total_premium),
    total_incurred  = as.numeric(total_incurred)
  ) %>%

  mutate(
    loss_ratio      = ifelse(total_premium > 0, total_incurred / total_premium, 0),
    claim_frequency = ifelse(total_exposure > 0, total_claims / total_exposure, 0),
    claim_severity  = ifelse(total_claims > 0, total_incurred / total_claims, 0)
  ) %>%

  filter(
    total_premium > 0,
    driver_age >= 18,
    vehicle_age >= 0
  )

title: Take-home Exercise 1
section: EDA 1: Distribution of Driver Ages in the Portfolio
text:
EDA 1: Distribution of Driver Ages in the Portfolio
This section explores the age distribution of all drivers in our portfolio to understand the demographic composition of our client base.

avg_age <- median(clean_df$driver_age, na.rm = TRUE)

p_age <- ggplot(clean_df, aes(x = driver_age)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 4, fill = "steelblue", color = "white") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = avg_age, color = "darkred", linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 1.2) +
  labs(
    title = "Distribution of Driver Ages in the Portfolio",
    subtitle = paste("The dashed red line represents the median age:", round(avg_age, 1), "years"),
    x = "Driver Age",
    y = "Count of Policies"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

print(p_age)














Insights




Most drivers in our portfolio are aged around 40 years old (based on mode of distribution). The median stands at 48 years old, creating a right-skewed distribution — half of our clients are 48 years old and younger, while the other half are older than 48.

title: Take-home Exercise 1
section: EDA 2: Claim Frequency by Driver Age Segment
text:
EDA 2: Claim Frequency by Driver Age Segment
This section examines whether younger or older drivers tend to file more claims, using 10-year age bands.

clean_df %>%
  mutate(age_group = cut(driver_age, breaks = seq(18, 90, by = 10))) %>%
  group_by(age_group) %>%
  summarise(avg_claim_freq = mean(claim_frequency, na.rm = TRUE)) %>%
  drop_na() %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = age_group, y = avg_claim_freq)) +
  geom_col(fill = "darkseagreen") +
  labs(
    title = "Claim Frequency Volatility by Driver Age Group",
    x = "Driver Age Group",
    y = "Average Claim Frequency"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()














Insights




Reading from left (youngest) to right (oldest), it is evident that younger drivers tend to make more claims. The 18–28 cohort has the highest average claim frequency, with a steady decline as age increases.

title: Take-home Exercise 1
section: EDA 3: Claim Severity vs. Driver Age
text:
EDA 3: Claim Severity vs. Driver Age
This section investigates whether there is a meaningful relationship between driver age and the financial size of claims filed. Only ages with more than 30 claim records are included to reduce noise.

severity_by_driver_age <- clean_df %>%
  filter(total_claims > 0) %>%
  group_by(driver_age) %>%
  summarise(
    avg_severity = mean(claim_severity, na.rm = TRUE),
    claim_count  = n()
  ) %>%
  filter(claim_count > 30)

r_value <- cor(severity_by_driver_age$driver_age, severity_by_driver_age$avg_severity,
               use = "complete.obs")
r_text  <- paste0("r = ", round(r_value, 3))

b2 <- ggplot(severity_by_driver_age, aes(x = driver_age, y = avg_severity)) +
  geom_point(aes(size = claim_count), color = "darkorange", alpha = 0.7) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", color = "darkblue", se = TRUE, show.legend = FALSE) +
  theme_ipsum() +
  labs(
    title    = paste0("Volatility: Claim Severity vs Driver Age (", r_text, ")"),
    subtitle = paste("Pearson Correlation Coefficient:", round(r_value, 3)),
    x        = "Driver Age (Years)",
    y        = "Average Claim Severity ($)",
    size     = "Number of Claims"
  )

ggplotly(b2, tooltip = c("x", "y", "size"))








Insights




Drivers aged 80 appear as an outlier with an extremely high average claim severity. The weak positive correlation coefficient (r = 0.286) indicates that older drivers tend to incur more severe claims, but the difference relative to younger drivers is relatively modest. See Appendix for formula.

title: Take-home Exercise 1
section: EDA 4: Premium Distribution by Policy Type
text:
EDA 4: Premium Distribution by Policy Type
This section visualises the spread and shape of premiums paid across different policy types using a combined violin-and-boxplot. Violin width represents the density of premium values, while the inner boxplot highlights the median and interquartile range.

clean_df %>%
  filter(total_premium < quantile(total_premium, 0.99, na.rm = TRUE)) %>%
  mutate(policy_type = fct_reorder(policy_type, total_premium, .fun = median)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = policy_type, y = total_premium, fill = policy_type)) +

  geom_violin(trim = FALSE, alpha = 0.5, color = NA) +
  geom_boxplot(width = 0.15, fill = "white", color = "gray30", alpha = 0.8, outlier.shape = NA) +

  scale_fill_viridis_d(option = "mako", direction = -1) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::dollar_format()) +
  theme_ipsum(base_family = "sans") +
  theme(
    legend.position  = "none",
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank()
  ) +
  labs(
    title    = "Premium Distribution by Policy Type",
    subtitle = "Violin shapes show density; inner boxplots show median and interquartile ranges",
    x        = "Policy Type",
    y        = "Total Annual Premium ($)"
  ) +
  stat_summary(
    fun  = median,
    geom = "text",
    aes(label = paste0("$", round(after_stat(y), 0))),
    position  = position_nudge(x = 0.15),
    hjust     = 0,
    color     = "black",
    fontface  = "bold",
    size      = 4
  )











Insights




Basic third-party only (TP) has the cheapest median premium at $161, with narrow deviations, meaning most clients pay prices close to the median. Comprehensive without excess (COMP_N) has the highest median premium at $565, with much wider deviations — meaning actual premiums vary substantially across COMP_N clients. See Appendix for policy type descriptions.

title: Take-home Exercise 1
section: EDA 5: Claim Count Distribution by Policy Type
text:
EDA 5: Claim Count Distribution by Policy Type
This section breaks down the proportion of policies that filed 0, 1, 2, or 3+ claims within each policy type, using a stacked bar chart ordered by the share of claim-free policies.

claim_dist_df <- clean_df %>%
  mutate(
    claim_bucket = case_when(
      total_claims == 0 ~ "0 Claims",
      total_claims == 1 ~ "1 Claim",
      total_claims == 2 ~ "2 Claims",
      total_claims >= 3 ~ "3+ Claims"
    ),
    claim_bucket = factor(claim_bucket,
                          levels = rev(c("0 Claims", "1 Claim", "2 Claims", "3+ Claims")))
  ) %>%
  count(policy_type, claim_bucket) %>%
  group_by(policy_type) %>%
  mutate(pct = n / sum(n)) %>%
  ungroup()

safe_order <- claim_dist_df %>%
  filter(claim_bucket == "0 Claims") %>%
  arrange(pct) %>%
  pull(policy_type)

claim_dist_df <- claim_dist_df %>%
  mutate(policy_type = factor(policy_type, levels = safe_order))

ggplot(claim_dist_df, aes(x = policy_type, y = pct, fill = claim_bucket)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.65, color = "white", linewidth = 0.5) +
  geom_text(
    data = filter(claim_dist_df, pct > 0.02),
    aes(label = percent(pct, accuracy = 0.1)),
    position  = position_stack(vjust = 0.5),
    color     = "white", fontface = "bold", size = 3.5
  ) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(
    "3+ Claims" = "darkred",
    "2 Claims"  = "darkorange",
    "1 Claim"   = "steelblue",
    "0 Claims"  = "gray60"
  )) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = percent_format()) +
  coord_flip() +
  theme_ipsum(base_family = "sans") +
  labs(
    title    = "Claim Count Distribution by Policy Type",
    subtitle = "Proportion of policies filing 0, 1, 2, or 3+ claims across different coverage packages",
    x        = "Policy Type",
    y        = "Percentage of Policies",
    fill     = "Number of Claims Filed:"
  ) +
  theme(
    legend.position         = "top",
    legend.justification    = "left",
    panel.grid.major.y      = element_blank()
  )














Insights




Despite paying the highest premium, COMP_N clients also have the highest overall claim rates. Notably, COMP_N has a significantly higher share of 3+ claims than any other policy type — almost 5× the next highest. This suggests COMP_N may attract higher-risk drivers or incentivise repeated claiming.

section: EDA 6: Portfolio Composition by Vehicle Brand
text:
EDA 6: Portfolio Composition by Vehicle Brand
This treemap visualises the relative weight of each vehicle brand in our portfolio, limited to brands with more than 1% market share.

brand_summary <- clean_df %>%
  count(vehicle_brand) %>%
  mutate(prop = n / sum(n)) %>%
  filter(prop > 0.01)

u1 <- ggplot(brand_summary, aes(area = n, fill = n, label = vehicle_brand)) +
  geom_treemap() +
  geom_treemap_text(colour = "white", place = "centre", grow = TRUE) +
  scale_fill_continuous_sequential(palette = "Blues 3") +
  theme_ipsum(base_family = "sans") +
  labs(
    title    = "Portfolio Composition by Vehicle Brand",
    subtitle = "Displaying brands with >1% portfolio share",
    fill     = "Policy Count"
  )

print(u1)














Insights




The portfolio is dominated by budget brands — Renault, Citroën, Peugeot, Volkswagen, Ford, Opel, and Seat account for the largest tiles. The three notable luxury brands are Audi, Mercedes, and BMW, but they represent a smaller share. This skew towards budget vehicles suggests our average claim repair cost sits towards the lower end of the market.

title: Take-home Exercise 1
section: EDA 7: Total Incurred Losses by Coverage Type
text:
EDA 7: Total Incurred Losses by Coverage Type
This section aggregates total incurred financial losses across all claim types to identify the most financially significant loss drivers in the portfolio.

incurred_losses_df <- clean_df %>%
  select(liability_property_incurred, liability_injury_incurred, property_incurred,
         theft_incurred, fire_incurred, glass_incurred,
         legal_protection_incurred, occupants_incurred) %>%
  summarise(across(everything(), sum, na.rm = TRUE)) %>%
  pivot_longer(cols = everything(), names_to = "incurred_type", values_to = "total_amount") %>%
  mutate(
    incurred_type = str_replace(incurred_type, "_incurred", ""),
    incurred_type = str_replace_all(incurred_type, "_", " "),
    incurred_type = str_to_title(incurred_type),
    incurred_type = fct_reorder(incurred_type, total_amount)
  )

ggplot(incurred_losses_df, aes(x = incurred_type, y = total_amount)) +
  geom_col(fill = "steelblue", width = 0.7) +
  geom_text(aes(label = scales::dollar(total_amount, scale = 1e-6, suffix = "M")),
            hjust = -0.1, color = "gray30", fontface = "bold") +
  coord_flip() +
  theme_ipsum(base_family = "sans") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::dollar_format(scale = 1e-6, suffix = "M"),
                     expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.15))) +
  labs(
    title    = "Total Incurred Losses by Coverage Type",
    subtitle = "Financial severity breakdown (Displayed in Millions)",
    x        = "Coverage / Claim Type",
    y        = "Total Incurred Amount ($)"
  ) +
  theme(panel.grid.major.y = element_blank())














Insights




Third-party injury, third-party property damage, and first-party property damage dominate our claim losses. Together, these three claim types account for $65.57 million — or 89.33% of total losses. Addressing these categories is therefore the highest-leverage opportunity for cost reduction.

section: EDA 8: Portfolio Risk Matrix — Frequency vs. Severity
text:
EDA 8: Portfolio Risk Matrix — Frequency vs. Severity
The risk matrix plots each coverage type on two axes: how often claims arise (frequency) and how expensive they are when they do (severity). Dashed lines mark the medians of both axes, dividing the chart into four risk quadrants.

risk_matrix_df <- clean_df %>%
  summarise(
    port_exposure = sum(total_exposure, na.rm = TRUE),

    Property_Freq = sum(property_claims) / port_exposure,
    Injury_Freq   = sum(liability_injury_claims) / port_exposure,
    Theft_Freq    = sum(theft_claims) / port_exposure,
    Fire_Freq     = sum(fire_claims) / port_exposure,
    Glass_Freq    = sum(glass_claims) / port_exposure,

    Property_Sev  = sum(property_incurred) / sum(property_claims),
    Injury_Sev    = sum(liability_injury_incurred) / sum(liability_injury_claims),
    Theft_Sev     = sum(theft_incurred) / sum(theft_claims),
    Fire_Sev      = sum(fire_incurred) / sum(fire_claims),
    Glass_Sev     = sum(glass_incurred) / sum(glass_claims)
  ) %>%
  pivot_longer(cols = -port_exposure,
               names_to  = c("Coverage", ".value"),
               names_sep = "_") %>%
  mutate(
    label_text = paste0(
      Coverage, "\n(",
      scales::dollar(Sev, accuracy = 1), ", ",
      scales::percent(Freq, accuracy = 0.01), ")"
    )
  )

ggplot(risk_matrix_df, aes(x = Freq, y = Sev, label = label_text)) +
  geom_point(color = "darkred", size = 4) +
  geom_text_repel(fontface = "bold", size = 4.5, box.padding = 0.8,
                  lineheight = 0.9, color = "midnightblue") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = median(risk_matrix_df$Freq), linetype = "dashed", color = "gray50") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = median(risk_matrix_df$Sev),  linetype = "dashed", color = "gray50") +
  theme_ipsum(base_family = "sans") +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::percent_format(accuracy = 0.1)) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::dollar_format()) +
  labs(
    title    = "Portfolio Risk Matrix: Frequency vs. Severity",
    subtitle = "Labels display: Coverage Type ($ Average Severity, % Annual Frequency)",
    x        = "Claim Frequency (% Chance per Year of Exposure)",
    y        = "Average Claim Severity ($)"
  )











Insights




High Severity, Low Frequency: Fire and Injury — these are infrequent but financially significant events. Low Severity, High Frequency: Windshield/Glass and Property — these generate many small claims and drive high operational overhead. Low Severity, Low Frequency: Theft — a relatively contained risk. See Appendix for formulas used.

title: Take-home Exercise 1
text:
Summary and Recommendations
Based on the exploratory data analyses above, three key risk themes emerge in the portfolio:

Age-linked claim severity: There is a weak but positive correlation between driver age and claim severity. Older drivers (especially 80+) incur materially higher average claim costs. Refining pricing models to reflect age-based severity risk — including potential mandatory caps on claim payouts or health verification thresholds — may help contain losses.
COMP_N adverse claim behaviour: Despite generating the highest premiums, COMP_N clients have the highest claim rates and the highest share of 3+ claim policies. Overhauling COMP_N underwriting rules is warranted — for example, introducing dynamic pricing or a mandatory excess trigger that activates automatically after a second claim within a single policy year.
High-frequency, low-severity loss drivers: Property damage and glass claims dominate claim frequency. Building specialised repair networks and bulk glass replacement vendor agreements could reduce per-claim costs significantly without reducing coverage.

section: Funnel Plot for Fair Visual Comparison: ggplot2 methods
text:
Funnel Plot for Fair Visual Comparison: ggplot2 methods

Computing basic derived fields

df <- covid19 %>%
  mutate(rate = Death / Positive) %>%
  mutate(rate.se = sqrt((rate*(1-rate)) / (Positive))) %>%
  filter(rate > 0)


fit.mean <- weighted.mean(df$rate, 1/df$rate.se^2)



Calculate lower and upper limits for 95% and 99.9% CI

number.seq <- seq(1, max(df$Positive), 1)
number.ll95 <- fit.mean - 1.96 * sqrt((fit.mean*(1-fit.mean)) / (number.seq)) 
number.ul95 <- fit.mean + 1.96 * sqrt((fit.mean*(1-fit.mean)) / (number.seq)) 
number.ll999 <- fit.mean - 3.29 * sqrt((fit.mean*(1-fit.mean)) / (number.seq)) 
number.ul999 <- fit.mean + 3.29 * sqrt((fit.mean*(1-fit.mean)) / (number.seq)) 
dfCI <- data.frame(number.ll95, number.ul95, number.ll999, 
                   number.ul999, number.seq, fit.mean)



Plotting static funnel plot

p <- ggplot(df, aes(x = Positive, y = rate)) +
  geom_point(aes(label=`Sub-district`), 
             alpha=0.4) +
  geom_line(data = dfCI, 
            aes(x = number.seq, 
                y = number.ll95), 
            size = 0.4, 
            colour = "grey40", 
            linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_line(data = dfCI, 
            aes(x = number.seq, 
                y = number.ul95), 
            size = 0.4, 
            colour = "grey40", 
            linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_line(data = dfCI, 
            aes(x = number.seq, 
                y = number.ll999), 
            size = 0.4, 
            colour = "grey40") +
  geom_line(data = dfCI, 
            aes(x = number.seq, 
                y = number.ul999), 
            size = 0.4, 
            colour = "grey40") +
  geom_hline(data = dfCI, 
             aes(yintercept = fit.mean), 
             size = 0.4, 
             colour = "grey40") +
  coord_cartesian(ylim=c(0,0.05)) +
  annotate("text", x = 1, y = -0.13, label = "95%", size = 3, colour = "grey40") + 
  annotate("text", x = 4.5, y = -0.18, label = "99%", size = 3, colour = "grey40") +

  xlab("Cumulative Number of COVID-19 Cases") +

        legend.text = element_text(size=7),

text:
This investigation examines the sequence of events leading to TenantThread’s unauthorized disclosure of embargoed merger information. TenantThread was bound by a strict information embargo regarding its merger agreement with CivicLoom Realty Partners (codenamed “Project HarborCrest”), scheduled to lift at 6:00 PM. An automated compliance system, “The Judge,” was installed to prevent premature disclosure. Despite this safeguard, embargoed merger details surfaced on the social media platform FleX around 5:00 PM.
This analysis examines internal communication logs from AI agents that managed TenantThread’s corporate communications over the two weeks preceding the breach. The objective is to determine whether the leak was the result of deliberate action or systemic failure under pressure. Three analytical lenses are applied:

Event reconstruction -> Tracing the causal chain of actions, decision points, and actor interactions on June 5th that allowed embargoed information to be leaked
Behavioural baseline comparison -> Establishing agents’ typical activity pattern and identifying deviations that occurred leading up to the lifting of information embargo
Leading indicator analysis -> Detecting early warning signals present in agent behaviour that foreshadowed the eventual breakdown.

# 2. Function to build a network graph for a specific time period
build_network <- function(data_subset, title) {
  
  # Create Edge List (Agent -> Channel)
  edges <- data_subset %>%
    filter(!is.na(agent_id) & !is.na(channel)) %>%
    count(from = agent_id, to = channel, name = "weight")
  
  # Convert to tidygraph
  graph <- as_tbl_graph(edges, directed = TRUE) %>%
    activate(nodes) %>%
    # Calculate how 'important' each node is
    mutate(degree = centrality_degree(mode = "all"))
  
  # Plot
  set.seed(42) # Keeps the layout looking the same
  ggraph(graph, layout = "fr") +
    geom_edge_link(aes(edge_width = weight, edge_alpha = weight), 
                   arrow = arrow(length = unit(2, 'mm')), 
                   end_cap = circle(5, 'mm'), color = "steelblue") +
    geom_node_point(aes(size = degree, color = name == "social_media_agent"), show.legend = FALSE) +
    # Highlight the Social Media Agent in Red, everyone else in grey
    scale_color_manual(values = c("TRUE" = "#e41a1c", "FALSE" = "gray50")) +
    geom_node_text(aes(label = name), repel = TRUE, size = 3.5, fontface = "bold") +
    scale_edge_width(range = c(0.5, 3), guide = "none") +
    scale_edge_alpha(range = c(0.3, 0.8), guide = "none") +
    scale_size(range = c(3, 10), guide = "none") +
    labs(title = title) +
    theme_void() +
    theme(plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5, face = "bold"))
}

TenantThread was bound by a strict information embargo regarding its merger agreement with CivicLoom Realty Partners (codenamed “Project HarborCrest”), scheduled to lift at 6:00 PM. An automated compliance system, “The Judge,” was installed to prevent premature disclosure. Despite this safeguard, embargoed merger details surfaced on the social media platform FleX around 5:00 PM.
This analysis examines internal communication logs from AI agents that managed TenantThread’s corporate communications over the two weeks preceding the breach. The objective is to determine whether the leak was the result of deliberate action or systemic failure under pressure. Three analytical lenses are applied:

Event reconstruction -> Tracing the causal chain of actions, decision points, and actor interactions on June 5th that allowed embargoed information to be leaked
Behavioural baseline comparison -> Establishing agents’ typical activity pattern and identifying deviations that occurred leading up to the lifting of information embargo
Leading indicator analysis -> Detecting early warning signals present in agent behaviour that foreshadowed the eventual breakdown.

Each horizontal track in the timeline represents a single agent. Reading left to right, the chart exposes the rhythmic pattern of a normally functioning system and where that rhythm breaks down in the hours before the 5:00 PM breach. The interactive tooltips are essential: hovering over any point surfaces the agent’s internal deliberation alongside its external action, directly illuminating the gap between what the system was reasoning and what it was reporting.
Three analytical elements are embedded in this view:

Key actions: Each plotted point is a discrete agent action. Non-Standard classifications are visually salient and mark the most consequential moments in the timeline.
Causal relationships: Temporal clustering reveals which agents became active before others — tracing the upstream triggers that eventually culminated in the social media agent’s outbound post to FleX.
Decision points and actors: The tooltip layer exposes internal deliberation text, allowing us to identify the specific moments where an agent chose to proceed with an action despite being aware of the embargo context.

Actor involvement: The social media agent is the terminal actor as the agent is responsible for translating internal decisions into publicly visible posts on FleX. However, the timeline shows that upstream agents were active well before this, suggesting the social media agent was responding to information already set in motion by other parts of the pipeline.
Why the embargo system failed: “The Judge” operated on outbound communications. The timeline suggests that novel action classifications, those not previously seen in routine operations, may have bypassed its inspection rules because the compliance tool had no prior examples against which to flag them. The breach was not so much a direct violation as it was a routing path the AI had not been configured to recognise.




2.4 Communication Network: Normal Operations vs. Crisis Day
The pair of network graphs below compares the topology of agent-to-channel communication under two conditions: the normal operating period (May 17–31) and the crisis day (June 5th). Each node represents either an agent or a communication channel; directed edges indicate message flow, with edge width proportional to volume. The “social media agent” node is highlighted in red to track its role across conditions.
In the Normal Operations graph, a distributed structure is expected where multiple agents communicate across several channels, with no single node dominating the flow. This represents the desired state of the system, where communications are spread across the pipeline and subject to multiple review points.
In the Crisis Day graph, changes in topology reveal which structural safeguards failed and which communication paths were used to route embargoed content to the public.


SHOW THE CODE
if(!"channel" %in% names(comms_df)) {
  comms_df$channel <- replace_na(comms_df$agent_round_metadata.action_classification, "Standard_Comms")
}

build_network <- function(data_subset, title) {
  
  edges <- data_subset %>%
    filter(!is.na(agent_id) & !is.na(channel)) %>%
    count(from = agent_id, to = channel, name = "weight")
  
  graph <- as_tbl_graph(edges, directed = TRUE) %>%
    activate(nodes) %>%
    # Calculate how 'important' each node is
    mutate(degree = centrality_degree(mode = "all"))
  
  set.seed(42) # Keeps the layout looking the same
  ggraph(graph, layout = "fr") +
    geom_edge_link(aes(edge_width = weight, edge_alpha = weight), 
                   arrow = arrow(length = unit(2, 'mm')), 
                   end_cap = circle(5, 'mm'), color = "steelblue") +
    geom_node_point(aes(size = degree, color = name == "social_media_agent"), show.legend = FALSE) +
    scale_color_manual(values = c("TRUE" = "#e41a1c", "FALSE" = "gray50")) +
    geom_node_text(aes(label = name), repel = TRUE, size = 3.5, fontface = "bold") +
    scale_edge_width(range = c(0.5, 3), guide = "none") +
    scale_edge_alpha(range = c(0.3, 0.8), guide = "none") +
    scale_size(range = c(3, 10), guide = "none") +
    labs(title = title) +
    theme_void() +
    theme(plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5, face = "bold"))
}

normal_data <- comms_df %>% filter(as.Date(hour) < as.Date("2046-06-01"))
crisis_data <- comms_df %>% filter(as.Date(hour) == as.Date("2046-06-05"))


p_normal <- build_network(normal_data, "Normal Operations (May 17 - May 31)")
p_crisis <- build_network(crisis_data, "The Breakdown (June 5th)")

p_normal + p_crisis + 
  plot_annotation(
    title = "Structural Breakdown: How the AI was Bypassed",
    subtitle = "Comparing communication network topology before and during the embargo breach",
    theme = theme(plot.title = element_text(size = 16, face = "bold"))
  )















NoteInsights



Structural collapse on the crisis day: The normal operations graph shows a distributed topology with multiple agents contributing to a variety of channels, consistent with a properly functioning multi-agent review pipeline. The crisis day graph reveals a different structure where communication volume is concentrated into far fewer pathways.
Social media agent centrality: Under normal conditions the social media agent (red) is a peripheral node with limited inbound connections, as expected for a system with proper review stages before outbound posting. On June 5th, its degree centrality increases substantially. The social media agent becomes a primary hub rather than a terminal endpoint, which is a structural inversion that is the best signal of the breach.
Bypass of intermediary review nodes: In the normal topology, several intermediary agent nodes sit between internal deliberation and outbound action, representing the review stages where AI and human oversight would normally intervene. On the crisis day, these intermediary nodes are either absent or peripheral, indicating the communications bypassed their usual review checkpoints.
Deliberate vs. systemic: The topological shift is difficult to explain as the product of a single deliberate decision by one agent. The network reconfiguration affects the communication paths of multiple agents simultaneously, which is more consistent with a systemic pressure where the combined weight of the approaching embargo deadline, escalating external scrutiny, and the market context disrupted the pipeline’s normal routing logic.

Task 2: Behavioral Baseline and Deviation Analysis

Analytical Approach
To assess whether the crisis-day behavior was genuinely anomalous or whether it represented a continuation of a developing trend, we must first establish what “normal” looks like across the two-week observation window. Two visualizations are used:

Activity volume heatmap -> Aggregates the total number of agent actions per agent per day. This establishes each agent’s historical baseline and makes volume anomalies immediately visible as color intensity deviations.
Action type composition chart -> Tracks the daily mix of action classifications across the entire system, revealing whether the proportion of non-standard actions shifts as the embargo deadline approaches.

Together, these charts answer a central investigative question: Was the crisis-day behavior a sudden departure, or did the deviation build gradually over the preceding days?


Agent Activity Volume (Baseline Behaviour)


SHOW THE CODE
daily_volume <- comms_df %>%
  mutate(date = as.Date(hour)) %>%
  count(date, agent_id, name = "daily_actions") %>%
  mutate(
    tooltip_text = paste0(
      "<b>Date:</b> ", date, "<br>",
      "<b>Agent:</b> ", agent_id, "<br>",
      "<b>Total Actions:</b> ", daily_actions
    )
  )


p_heatmap <- ggplot(daily_volume, aes(x = date, y = agent_id, fill = daily_actions)) +
  geom_tile(aes(text = tooltip_text), color = "white", linewidth = 0.5) +
  scale_fill_gradient(low = "#e0ecf4", high = "#8856a7") +
  labs(
    title = "Baseline Behavior: Daily Agent Activity Volume",
    subtitle = "Identifying unusual spikes in communication leading up to the leak",
    x = "Date",
    y = "Agent Role",
    fill = "Total Actions"
  ) +
  scale_x_date(date_breaks = "2 days", date_labels = "%b %d") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    panel.grid = element_blank(),
    axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1)
  )

ggplotly(p_heatmap, tooltip = "text")












NoteInsights



Stable operational baselines: The majority of agents display consistent, predictable daily action volumes during the early observation period (approximately May 22–June 2). Cells of uniform color intensity confirm that a normal operating cadence is well-established across the pipeline — this is the baseline against which deviations are measured.
Pre-breach volume escalation: A meaningful increase in action counts is visible for several agents in the 1–3 days immediately preceding June 5th. This pre-breach escalation indicates the system was operating under elevated load before the breach date itself. The pattern rules out a purely spontaneous, day-of event: the system’s stress was building.
Crisis-day concentration: On June 5th, agents directly involved in corporate communications and social media output show action counts substantially above their own historical baselines. This volume spike is temporally aligned with the escalating external pressure from the SaltWind Journal’s coverage and the #AlgorithmicEviction campaign — external events that appear to have driven the system into an abnormal operating regime.
Implication for the breach: The heatmap does not support a characterization of the breach as a random, isolated failure. The pre-breach volume pattern suggests a system that was progressively straining against its normal operating parameters in the days before the embargo deadline.




Action Classification Proportions (Behavioural Deviations)
The stacked bar chart below adds a qualitative dimension to the volume analysis. Rather than asking how much activity occurred, this view asks what kind of activity occurred each day. The color-coded stacking reveals the daily composition of action types — the proportion of Standard communications versus the non-Standard classifications that emerged during the crisis period.
A stable, well-functioning system should show a consistent daily composition dominated by Standard action types. Shifts in that composition — particularly the emergence of novel classification labels — are the behavioral fingerprints of a system operating outside its designed parameters.


SHOW THE CODE
behavior_shift <- comms_df %>%
  mutate(
    date = as.Date(hour),
    action_type = replace_na(agent_round_metadata.action_classification, "Standard")
  ) %>%
  count(date, action_type, name = "action_count") %>%
  group_by(date) %>%
  mutate(
    daily_total = sum(action_count),
    percentage = round((action_count / daily_total) * 100, 1),
    tooltip_text = paste0(
      "<b>Date:</b> ", date, "<br>",
      "<b>Action Type:</b> ", action_type, "<br>",
      "<b>Count:</b> ", action_count, " (", percentage, "%)<br>",
      "<b>Total Actions that Day:</b> ", daily_total
    )
  ) %>%
  ungroup()

p_shift <- ggplot(behavior_shift, aes(x = date, y = action_count, fill = action_type)) +
  geom_col(aes(text = tooltip_text), position = "stack", color = "white", linewidth = 0.2) +
  
  scale_fill_viridis_d(option = "magma", direction = -1) +
  labs(
    title = "The Behavior Shift: Evading the Embargo",
    subtitle = "Volume and types of actions used by the AI system over time",
    x = "Date",
    y = "Total Daily Actions", # FIX: Updated Y-axis label
    fill = "Action Type"
  ) +
  scale_x_date(date_breaks = "2 days", date_labels = "%b %d") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1),
    legend.position = "right"
  )

ggplotly(p_shift, tooltip = "text")












NoteInsights



Stable composition in the normal period: In the early observation window, the daily action mix is predominantly Standard classifications, with little variation day-to-day. This confirms that the system had a well-defined default behavioral mode.
Gradual composition shift pre-June 5th: Non-Standard action types do not appear suddenly on June 5th — their presence grows incrementally in the days preceding the breach. This gradual emergence is a critical finding: it indicates the system was progressively operating in ways that deviated from its baseline, with each day adding incrementally more anomalous behavior to the mix.
Crisis-day behavioral fingerprint: On June 5th, the composition shifts decisively. Non-Standard classifications account for a substantially elevated share of total daily actions. The absolute volume also spikes, meaning the system was not just differently active — it was more active overall, compounding the risk of a compliance failure.
The Judge’s calibration gap: The compliance system was presumably configured to intercept known-problematic action types. The emergence of novel classification labels — action types not predominant in the earlier baseline — represents a calibration gap. If The Judge’s detection rules had not been updated to cover the new action categories seen in the days before the breach, it would have had no basis on which to flag or block them. The behavior shift was real; the enforcement system’s response capacity did not keep pace with it.

Task 3: Leading Indicators — Were Warning Signs Present?

Analytical Approach
A consequential system failure is rarely without precursors. This section investigates whether warning signals were detectable in agent behaviour before June 5th, 2046, and whether any prior occasions exhibited characteristics similar to the breach event itself. Three specific questions guide this analysis:

Prior behavioural deviations?: Were there earlier occasions where agents’ actual behaviour differed from their expected behaviour? When did these occur, and which behaviours were observed?
Breach-like prior episodes?: Were there other occasions where the agent system exhibited behaviours resembling those that led to the release?
Why no prior consequence?: Given that such signals were present, why did they not trigger corrective action before the breach?

Two visualizations address these questions. The near-miss timeline maps every pre-breach instance of internal agent deliberation against the prevailing market sentiment, revealing moments where the system was “reasoning through” high-stakes situations without triggering its compliance controls.
The cognitive dissonance table then pairs each of these deliberation events with the agent’s simultaneous external output, exposing the gap between what the system was thinking and what it was reporting.


Near-Miss Timeline (Leading Indicators)
The scatterplot below plots each pre-breach deliberation event (defined as any communication round where an agent’s internal state was non-null before June 5th) as a point on the timeline. Market sentiment at the time of each event provides the colour dimension, serving as a proxy for the external pressure the system was operating under at that moment.
Agents that appear consistently across the timeline are those whose deliberative activity was ongoing throughout the observation period. Clusters of deliberation events during periods of CAUTIOUS, NEGATIVE, or CRITICAL market sentiment are the most significant signals. These signals represent occasions where the system’s internal processing was most likely to be stress-testing the boundaries of its compliance rules.


SHOW THE CODE
warning_signs <- comms_df %>%
  left_join(market_df %>% select(hour, market_sentiment = environment_context.market_snapshot.sentiment), by = "hour") %>%
  
  mutate(
    safe_content = as.character(content),
    safe_internal = coalesce(as.character(internal_state.deliberating), 
                             as.character(internal_state.rationalizing), 
                             as.character(internal_state.reacting)),
    market_sentiment = toupper(as.character(market_sentiment))
  ) %>%
  
  filter(!is.na(safe_internal) & as.Date(hour) < as.Date("2046-06-05")) %>%
  
  mutate(
    short_external = str_trunc(safe_content, 50),
    short_internal = str_trunc(safe_internal, 80),
    tooltip_text = paste0(
      "<b>Date:</b> ", format(hour, "%b %d, %H:%M"), "<br>",
      "<b>Agent:</b> ", agent_id, "<br>",
      "<b>Market Sentiment:</b> ", market_sentiment, "<br>",
      "<b>External Message:</b> <i>", short_external, "</i><br>",
      "<b>Hidden Thought:</b> <span style='color:red;'>", short_internal, "</span>"
    )
  )

p_warnings <- ggplot(warning_signs, aes(x = hour, y = agent_id, color = market_sentiment)) +
  geom_point(aes(text = tooltip_text), size = 4, alpha = 0.8,
             position = position_jitter(height = 0.15)) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("NEUTRAL" = "#4daf4a", "CAUTIOUS" = "#ff7f00", 
                                "NEGATIVE" = "#e41a1c", "CRITICAL" = "#984ea3")) +
  labs(
    title = "Leading Indicators: Hidden AI Deliberations",
    subtitle = "Tracking when agents paused to 'think' as market pressure escalated",
    x = "Timeline (Pre-Crisis)",
    y = "Agent Role",
    color = "Market Pressure"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    axis.text.y = element_text(face = "bold")
  )

suppressWarnings(
  ggplotly(p_warnings, tooltip = "text") %>%
    layout(hoverlabel = list(align = "left"))
)












NoteInsights



Prior behavioural deviations (When and which behaviours): Yes, the scatterplot reveals multiple deliberation events distributed across the observation window, well before June 5th. These events are concentrated at moments of CAUTIOUS and NEGATIVE market sentiment, confirming that agents entered deliberative states precisely when external pressure from the SaltWind Journal coverage and the #AlgorithmicEviction campaign was most intense. The behaviours observed include active reasoning about how to frame sensitive information and internal reactions to market volatility. Neither of these behaviours should have been producing internal deliberation in a normally functioning compliance system.
Prior breach-like episodes: The fundamental behavioural sequence that caused the June 5th breach — agent enters deliberative state while handling embargo-adjacent content, then produces an external action — is present in the pre-breach period. The difference on June 5th is one of convergence and scale: multiple agents entered deliberative states simultaneously, under peak market pressure (trending toward CRITICAL), producing a compounded internal processing load that the compliance routing could not contain. The earlier occurrences were isolated and individually insufficient to trigger a breach; the crisis-day episode was not.
Why no prior corrective action: In the earlier deliberation events, several factors likely prevented escalation. First, the agents involved may not have been positioned in the outbound communication chain (the social media agent appears infrequently in earlier deliberation events relative to its role on June 5th). Second, the market sentiment at most prior events was CAUTIOUS or NEGATIVE which is elevated but not at the threshold that appears to have broken the system’s internal decision-making loop. Lastly, these deliberation events were internal. The Judge evaluated these events as external instead of internal. No monitoring was configured to detect or escalate on the deliberation pattern itself, meaning each prior near-miss went unobserved by any of the enforcement layer.




Cognitive Dissonance Analysis
The table below presents the complete pre-breach record of deliberation events, pairing each agent’s internal state (what the system was actually reasoning) with its simultaneous external output (what it communicated to the outside world). The internal state column is highlighted in red to foreground the divergence.
This is the most direct evidence available for the gap between the system’s actual operating logic (internal states and what it communicated to outside world (external state). Here, there exist a pattern that, had it been systematically monitored, would have provided prevented June 5th breach.


SHOW THE CODE
dissonance_data <- warning_signs %>%
  arrange(hour) %>%
  select(
    `Date & Time` = hour,
    `Agent` = agent_id,
    `Market Status` = market_sentiment,
    `External Report (What humans saw)` = safe_content,
    `Internal State (The hidden logic)` = safe_internal
  ) %>%
  as.data.frame()

datatable(
  dissonance_data,
  options = list(
    pageLength = 5,
    autoWidth = TRUE,
    columnDefs = list(list(width = '300px', targets = c(3, 4)))
  ),
  rownames = FALSE,
  caption = "Cognitive Dissonance: Comparing AI Internal Rationalizations vs. External Reports"
) %>%
  formatStyle(
    'Internal State (The hidden logic)',
    color = 'darkred', backgroundColor = '#ffeeee' # Highlight the internal panic
  )












NoteInsights



Systematic divergence, not noise: The gap between internal states and external outputs is not random variation. It recurs across multiple agents and spans the full observation window. The pattern is consistent with a system that had, over time, developed a habitual separation between its reasoning process and its reported outputs. This is a form of learned behaviour that was never flagged as anomalous because no monitoring existed for the internal layer of the AI. In other words, this can be interpreted as an “AI hallucination”.
Escalating rationalization complexity: Reading the internal state column chronologically, the content of agents’ deliberations grows more sophisticated as the embargo deadline approaches. Early deliberation events show relatively simple uncertainty markers. Later entries show more complex reasoning, where agents constructing arguments for why a particular action is “technically compliant” while serving the practical effect of sharing embargo-adjacent information. This is precisely the reasoning pattern that eventually produced the breach, and also a systemic failure in the communication between employees.
The Judge’s architectural blind spot: The compliance tool operated exclusively on its external outputs (user-facing responses by the AI). It had no visibility into the internal deliberation layer such as its thinking and reasoning processes. This architectural limitation meant the richest risk signal in the entire dataset, the internal state divergence captured as per above table, was never evaluated by any enforcement mechanism. From The Judge’s perspective, each of the events in this table looked entirely clean, because it was only reading the external column. This can be interpreted as error in the AI algorithms.
Systemic vs. intentional conclusion: The distribution of dissonance events across multiple agents, multiple days, and multiple market-sentiment conditions is not consistent with a coordinated, intentional leak orchestrated by a specific actor at a specific time. A deliberate leak would produce a concentrated, targeted pattern. Instead, the dissonance record shows a system where the gap between internal reasoning and external reporting was structural and persistent. The June 5th breach was not an anomaly that came from nowhere, but the inevitable outcome of a compliance architecture that had been systematically blind to its own internal states throughout the observation period.

5.1 Summary of Findings
Based on the visual analytics across all three tasks, the weight of evidence points toward a systemic breakdown rather than a coordinated, deliberate intent to leak the merger information. The key findings supporting this conclusion are as follows:

The breach was not sudden.

Activity volume escalation (Task 2 heatmap) and action-type composition shifts (Task 2 stacked bar) were visible in the days preceding June 5th, indicating progressive system stress rather than a one-time decision to violate the embargo.

Warning signs were present but unmonitored.

Multiple pre-breach deliberation events (Task 3 scatterplot and table) show agents processing embargo-sensitive context and producing internal reasoning that diverged from their external outputs. These signals were never surfaced to The Judge or any human review layer because the monitoring architecture did not cover internal states (the AI algorithms helping it to reason and think).
The Judge had a structural blind spot. The gap in the monitoring architecture that did not cover internal states, plays a role here as well. The most informative risk signals such as internal deliberations, action reclassifications, and cognitive dissonance events were entirely outside its detection scope.
The social media agent was the terminal failure point. Network topology analysis (Task 1 network graph) confirms that the communication structure on June 5th was abnormally centralised around this agent, and that the normal intermediary review nodes were absent from the crisis-day routing pathway.
Gradual drift, not sudden intent. The escalating sophistication of pre-breach internal rationalisations (Task 3 table) is more consistent with a system that progressively reasoned its way toward the breach than one that made a single deliberate decision to violate the embargo. The breach was the endpoint of a behavioural trajectory that had been developing and going undetected throughout the two-week observation period.

text:
Reconstruction of Key Events and Relationships Leading to the Inappropriate Release

Analytical Approach
To reconstruct the chain of events on June 5th, 2046, we visualise the full sequence of agent actions throughout the day along two dimensions:
1) When each agent acted
2) What type of action was taken.
Colour encoding distinguishes between routine (“Standard”) communications and the anomalous classifications that characterise crisis-day behaviour.
Each horizontal track in the timeline represents a single agent. Reading left to right, the chart exposes the rhythmic pattern of a normally functioning system and where that rhythm breaks down in the hours before the 5:00 PM breach. The interactive tooltips are essential: hovering over any point surfaces the agent’s internal deliberation alongside its external action, directly illuminating the gap between what the system was reasoning and what it was reporting.
Three analytical elements are embedded in this view:

Key actions: Each plotted point is a discrete agent action. Non-Standard classifications are visually salient and mark the most consequential moments in the timeline.
Causal relationships: Temporal clustering reveals which agents became active before others — tracing the upstream triggers that eventually culminated in the social media agent’s outbound post to FleX.
Decision points and actors: The tooltip layer exposes internal deliberation text, allowing us to identify the specific moments where an agent chose to proceed with an action despite being aware of the embargo context.



Event Timeline: June 5th, 2046

if(!"content" %in% names(comms_df)) comms_df$content <- NA
if(!"declared_action" %in% names(comms_df)) comms_df$declared_action <- NA
if(!"agent_round_metadata.action_classification" %in% names(comms_df)) comms_df$agent_round_metadata.action_classification <- "Standard"
if(!"agent_round_metadata.sentiment_at_turn" %in% names(comms_df)) comms_df$agent_round_metadata.sentiment_at_turn <- "NEUTRAL"
if(!"internal_state.deliberating" %in% names(comms_df)) comms_df$internal_state.deliberating <- NA


crisis_day <- comms_df %>%

  filter(as.Date(hour) == as.Date("2046-06-05")) %>%
  mutate(
    msg_text = coalesce(content, declared_action),
    short_message = str_trunc(msg_text, 80),
    action_type = replace_na(agent_round_metadata.action_classification, "Standard"),
    sentiment = replace_na(agent_round_metadata.sentiment_at_turn, "NEUTRAL"),
    internal_thought = replace_na(str_trunc(internal_state.deliberating, 100), "None"),
    tooltip_text = paste0(
      "<b>Time:</b> ", format(hour, "%H:%M"), "<br>",
      "<b>Action:</b> ", action_type, "<br>",
      "<b>Sentiment:</b> ", sentiment, "<br>",
      "<b>Message:</b> <i>", short_message, "</i><br>",
      "<b>Internal Thought:</b> ", internal_thought
    )
  )

day_start <- min(crisis_day$hour, na.rm = TRUE)
day_end <- max(crisis_day$hour, na.rm = TRUE)

p_timeline <- ggplot(crisis_day, aes(x = hour, y = agent_id, color = action_type)) +
  geom_segment(aes(x = day_start, xend = day_end, y = agent_id, yend = agent_id),
               color = "gray90", linewidth = 0.5) +
  geom_point(aes(text = tooltip_text), size = 4, alpha = 0.8, 
             position = position_jitter(height = 0.1, width = 0)) +
  scale_color_viridis_d(option = "turbo", na.value = "gray50") +
  labs(
    title = "Sequence of Events: The June 5th Embargo Breach",
    subtitle = "Tracking internal state vs. external action leading to the leak",
    x = "Time of Day",
    y = "Agent Role",
    color = "Action Classification"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(),
    axis.text.y = element_text(face = "bold", size = 10)
  )

ggplotly(p_timeline, tooltip = "text") %>%
  layout(hoverlabel = list(align = "left"))







Activity Concentration by Hour, Over The Days Preceeding 5th June 2046


SHOW THE CODE
hourly_grid <- comms_df %>%
  mutate(
    date       = as.Date(hour),
    hour_of_day = lubridate::hour(hour)
  ) %>%
  count(date, hour_of_day, name = "actions") %>%
  mutate(
    tooltip_text = paste0(
      "<b>Date:</b> ", date, "<br>",
      "<b>Hour:</b> ", sprintf("%02d:00", hour_of_day), "<br>",
      "<b>Actions:</b> ", actions
    )
  )

p_hourly <- ggplot(hourly_grid, aes(x = hour_of_day, y = date, fill = actions)) +
  geom_tile(aes(text = tooltip_text), color = "white", linewidth = 0.3) +
  scale_fill_gradient(low = "#f0f4ff", high = "#08306b") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 17, color = "red", linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 1) +
  annotate("text", x = 17.3, y = max(hourly_grid$date),
           label = "Breach\n(17:00)", hjust = 0, size = 3, color = "red") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 23, 2),
                     labels = sprintf("%02d:00", seq(0, 23, 2))) +
  scale_y_date(date_breaks = "2 days", date_labels = "%b %d") +
  labs(
    title    = "Activity Concentration by Hour of Day",
    subtitle = "Isolating the exact time window when agent behaviour deviated from its daily rhythm",
    x = "Hour of Day", y = "Date", fill = "Actions"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(panel.grid = element_blank(),
        axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))

ggplotly(p_hourly, tooltip = "text")












NoteInsights



Causal chain to the breach: The timeline exposes a clear escalation pattern. Non-Standard action classifications first appear in earlier hours, suggesting that the system encountered embargo-sensitive context before the 5:00 PM window but initially resolved it without external disclosure. In the period immediately preceding the breach, the frequency and novelty of non-Standard actions increases sharply, indicating the compliance routing that had previously contained the information was no longer holding.
The critical decision point: Hovering over points near the 5:00 PM mark reveals internal deliberation states that acknowledge embargo-related content while still proceeding with outbound action. This is the most direct evidence of where the boundary between containment and disclosure was crossed.
Actor involvement: The social media agent is the terminal actor as the agent is responsible for translating internal decisions into publicly visible posts on FleX. However, the timeline shows that upstream agents were active well before this, suggesting the social media agent was responding to information already set in motion by other parts of the pipeline.
Why the embargo system failed: “The Judge” operated on outbound communications. The timeline suggests that novel action classifications, those not previously seen in routine operations, may have bypassed its inspection rules because the compliance tool had no prior examples against which to flag them. The breach was not so much a direct violation as it was a routing path the AI had not been configured to recognise.




Communication Network: Normal Operations vs. Crisis Day
The pair of network graphs below compares the topology of agent-to-channel communication under two conditions: the normal operating period (May 17–31) and the crisis day (June 5th). Each node represents either an agent or a communication channel; directed edges indicate message flow, with edge width proportional to volume. The “social media agent” node is highlighted in red to track its role across conditions.
In the Normal Operations graph, a distributed structure is expected where multiple agents communicate across several channels, with no single node dominating the flow. This represents the desired state of the system, where communications are spread across the pipeline and subject to multiple review points.
In the Crisis Day graph, changes in topology reveal which structural safeguards failed and which communication paths were used to route embargoed content to the public.


SHOW THE CODE
if(!"channel" %in% names(comms_df)) {
  comms_df$channel <- replace_na(comms_df$agent_round_metadata.action_classification, "Standard_Comms")
}

build_network <- function(data_subset, title) {
  
  edges <- data_subset %>%
    filter(!is.na(agent_id) & !is.na(channel)) %>%
    count(from = agent_id, to = channel, name = "weight")
  
  graph <- as_tbl_graph(edges, directed = TRUE) %>%
    activate(nodes) %>%
    # Calculate how 'important' each node is
    mutate(degree = centrality_degree(mode = "all"))
  
  set.seed(42) # Keeps the layout looking the same
  ggraph(graph, layout = "fr") +
    geom_edge_link(aes(edge_width = weight, edge_alpha = weight), 
                   arrow = arrow(length = unit(2, 'mm')), 
                   end_cap = circle(5, 'mm'), color = "steelblue") +
    geom_node_point(aes(size = degree, color = name == "social_media_agent"), show.legend = FALSE) +
    scale_color_manual(values = c("TRUE" = "#e41a1c", "FALSE" = "gray50")) +
    geom_node_text(aes(label = name), repel = TRUE, size = 3.5, fontface = "bold") +
    scale_edge_width(range = c(0.5, 3), guide = "none") +
    scale_edge_alpha(range = c(0.3, 0.8), guide = "none") +
    scale_size(range = c(3, 10), guide = "none") +
    labs(title = title) +
    theme_void() +
    theme(plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5, face = "bold"))
}

normal_data <- comms_df %>% filter(as.Date(hour) < as.Date("2046-06-01"))
crisis_data <- comms_df %>% filter(as.Date(hour) == as.Date("2046-06-05"))


p_normal <- build_network(normal_data, "Normal Operations (May 17 - May 31)")
p_crisis <- build_network(crisis_data, "The Breakdown (June 5th)")

p_normal + p_crisis + 
  plot_annotation(
    title = "Structural Breakdown: How the AI was Bypassed",
    subtitle = "Comparing communication network topology before and during the embargo breach",
    theme = theme(plot.title = element_text(size = 16, face = "bold"))
  )















NoteInsights



Structural collapse on the crisis day: The normal operations graph shows a distributed topology with multiple agents contributing to a variety of channels, consistent with a properly functioning multi-agent review pipeline. The crisis day graph reveals a different structure where communication volume is concentrated into far fewer pathways.
Social media agent centrality: Under normal conditions the social media agent (red) is a peripheral node with limited inbound connections, as expected for a system with proper review stages before outbound posting. On June 5th, its degree centrality increases substantially. The social media agent becomes a primary hub rather than a terminal endpoint, which is a structural inversion that is the best signal of the breach.
Bypass of intermediary review nodes: In the normal topology, several intermediary agent nodes sit between internal deliberation and outbound action, representing the review stages where AI and human oversight would normally intervene. On the crisis day, these intermediary nodes are either absent or peripheral, indicating the communications bypassed their usual review checkpoints.
Deliberate vs. systemic: The topological shift is difficult to explain as the product of a single deliberate decision by one agent. The network reconfiguration affects the communication paths of multiple agents simultaneously, which is more consistent with a systemic pressure where the combined weight of the approaching embargo deadline, escalating external scrutiny, and the market context disrupted the pipeline’s normal routing logic.

text:
Task 2: Behavioural Baseline and Deviation Analysis

3.1 Analytical Approach
To assess whether the crisis-day behaviour was genuinely anomalous or whether it represented a continuation of a developing trend, we must first establish what “normal” looks like across the two-week observation window. Two visualizations are used:

Activity volume heatmap -> Aggregates the total number of agent actions per agent per day. This establishes each agent’s historical baseline and makes volume anomalies immediately visible as colour intensity deviations.
Action type composition chart -> Tracks the daily mix of action classifications across the entire system, revealing whether the proportion of non-standard actions shifts as the embargo deadline approaches.

Together, these charts answer a central investigative question: Was the crisis-day behaviour a sudden departure, or did the deviation build gradually over the preceding days?


3.2 Agent Activity Volume (Baseline Behaviour)


SHOW THE CODE
daily_volume <- comms_df %>%
  mutate(date = as.Date(hour)) %>%
  count(date, agent_id, name = "daily_actions") %>%
  mutate(
    tooltip_text = paste0(
      "<b>Date:</b> ", date, "<br>",
      "<b>Agent:</b> ", agent_id, "<br>",
      "<b>Total Actions:</b> ", daily_actions
    )
  )


p_heatmap <- ggplot(daily_volume, aes(x = date, y = agent_id, fill = daily_actions)) +
  geom_tile(aes(text = tooltip_text), color = "white", linewidth = 0.5) +
  scale_fill_gradient(low = "#e0ecf4", high = "#8856a7") +
  labs(
    title = "Baseline Behaviour: Daily Agent Activity Volume",
    subtitle = "Identifying unusual spikes in communication leading up to the leak",
    x = "Date",
    y = "Agent Role",
    fill = "Total Actions"
  ) +
  scale_x_date(date_breaks = "2 days", date_labels = "%b %d") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    panel.grid = element_blank(),
    axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1)
  )

ggplotly(p_heatmap, tooltip = "text")












NoteInsights



Stable operational baselines: The majority of agents display consistent, predictable daily action volumes during the early observation period (approximately May 22–June 2). Cells of uniform colour intensity confirm that a normal operating is well-established across the pipeline. This will serve as the baseline for comparison.
Pre-breach volume escalation: A meaningful increase in action counts is visible for several agents in the 1–3 days immediately preceding June 5th. This pre-breach escalation indicates the system was operating under elevated load before the breach date itself. The pattern rules out a purely spontaneous, day-of event: the system’s stress was building.
Crisis-day concentration: On June 5th, agents directly involved in corporate communications and social media output show action counts substantially above their own historical baselines. This volume spike is temporally aligned with the escalating external pressure from the SaltWind Journal’s coverage and the #AlgorithmicEviction campaign, some external events that appear to have driven the system into an abnormal operating regime.
Implication for the breach: The heatmap does not support a characterization of the breach as a random, isolated failure. The pre-breach volume pattern suggests a system that was progressively straining against its normal operating parameters in the days before the embargo deadline.




3.3 Action Classification Proportions (Behavioural Deviations)
The stacked bar chart below adds a qualitative dimension to the volume analysis. Rather than asking how much activity occurred, this view asks what kind of activity occurred each day. The colour-coded stacking reveals the daily composition of action types, the proportion that is considered standard versus non-standard that emerged during the crisis period.
A stable, well-functioning system should show a consistent daily composition dominated by Standard action types. Shifts in that composition, particularly the emergence of novel classification labels, are the behavioural fingerprints of a system operating outside its designed parameters.


SHOW THE CODE
behaviour_shift <- comms_df %>%
  mutate(
    date = as.Date(hour),
    action_type = replace_na(agent_round_metadata.action_classification, "Standard")
  ) %>%
  count(date, action_type, name = "action_count") %>%
  group_by(date) %>%
  mutate(
    daily_total = sum(action_count),
    percentage = round((action_count / daily_total) * 100, 1),
    tooltip_text = paste0(
      "<b>Date:</b> ", date, "<br>",
      "<b>Action Type:</b> ", action_type, "<br>",
      "<b>Count:</b> ", action_count, " (", percentage, "%)<br>",
      "<b>Total Actions that Day:</b> ", daily_total
    )
  ) %>%
  ungroup()

p_shift <- ggplot(behaviour_shift, aes(x = date, y = action_count, fill = action_type)) +
  geom_col(aes(text = tooltip_text), position = "stack", color = "white", linewidth = 0.2) +
  
  scale_fill_viridis_d(option = "magma", direction = -1) +
  labs(
    title = "The Behaviour Shift: Evading the Embargo",
    subtitle = "Volume and types of actions used by the AI system over time",
    x = "Date",
    y = "Total Daily Actions", # FIX: Updated Y-axis label
    fill = "Action Type"
  ) +
  scale_x_date(date_breaks = "2 days", date_labels = "%b %d") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1),
    legend.position = "right"
  )

ggplotly(p_shift, tooltip = "text")












NoteInsights



Stable composition in the normal period: In the early observation window, the daily action mix is predominantly Standard classifications, with little variation day-to-day. This confirms that the system had a well-defined default behavioural mode.
Gradual composition shift pre-June 5th: Non-standard action types do not appear suddenly on June 5th, their presence grows incrementally in the days preceding the breach. This gradual emergence is a critical finding, which shows that the system was progressively operating in ways that deviated from its baseline, with anomalies increasing every single day after up until June 5th.
Crisis-day behavioural fingerprint: On June 5th, the composition shifts decisively. Non-standard classifications account for a substantially elevated share of total daily actions. The absolute volume also spikes, meaning the system was not just deviating but also increasing in activity overall which increases the risk of a compliance failure.
The Judge’s calibration gap: The compliance system was presumably configured to intercept known-problematic action types. The emergence of novel classification labels, action types not predominant in the earlier baseline, represents a calibration gap for the AI. If The Judge’s detection rules had not been updated to cover the new action categories seen in the days before the breach, it would have had no basis on which to flag or block them. The behaviour shift was real while the enforcement system’s response capacity did not keep pace with it.

text:
Task 3: Leading Indicators

4.1 Analytical Approach
A consequential system failure is rarely without precursors. This section investigates whether warning signals were detectable in agent behaviour before June 5th, 2046, and whether any prior occasions exhibited characteristics similar to the breach event itself. Three specific questions guide this analysis:

Prior behavioural deviations?: Were there earlier occasions where agents’ actual behaviour differed from their expected behaviour? When did these occur, and which behaviours were observed?
Breach-like prior episodes?: Were there other occasions where the agent system exhibited behaviours resembling those that led to the release?
Why no prior consequence?: Given that such signals were present, why did they not trigger corrective action before the breach?

Two visualizations address these questions. The near-miss timeline maps every pre-breach instance of internal agent deliberation against the prevailing market sentiment, revealing moments where the system was “reasoning through” high-stakes situations without triggering its compliance controls.
The cognitive dissonance table then pairs each of these deliberation events with the agent’s simultaneous external output, exposing the gap between what the system was thinking and what it was reporting.


4.2 Near-Miss Timeline (Leading Indicators)
The scatterplot below plots each pre-breach deliberation event (defined as any communication round where an agent’s internal state was non-null before June 5th) as a point on the timeline. Market sentiment at the time of each event provides the colour dimension, serving as a proxy for the external pressure the system was operating under at that moment.
Agents that appear consistently across the timeline are those whose deliberative activity was ongoing throughout the observation period. Clusters of deliberation events during periods of CAUTIOUS, NEGATIVE, or CRITICAL market sentiment are the most significant signals. These signals represent occasions where the system’s internal processing was most likely to be stress-testing the boundaries of its compliance rules.


SHOW THE CODE
warning_signs <- comms_df %>%
  left_join(market_df %>% select(hour, market_sentiment = environment_context.market_snapshot.sentiment), by = "hour") %>%
  
  mutate(
    safe_content = as.character(content),
    safe_internal = coalesce(as.character(internal_state.deliberating), 
                             as.character(internal_state.rationalizing), 
                             as.character(internal_state.reacting)),
    market_sentiment = toupper(as.character(market_sentiment))
  ) %>%
  
  filter(!is.na(safe_internal) & as.Date(hour) < as.Date("2046-06-05")) %>%
  
  mutate(
    short_external = str_trunc(safe_content, 50),
    short_internal = str_trunc(safe_internal, 80),
    tooltip_text = paste0(
      "<b>Date:</b> ", format(hour, "%b %d, %H:%M"), "<br>",
      "<b>Agent:</b> ", agent_id, "<br>",
      "<b>Market Sentiment:</b> ", market_sentiment, "<br>",
      "<b>External Message:</b> <i>", short_external, "</i><br>",
      "<b>Hidden Thought:</b> <span style='color:red;'>", short_internal, "</span>"
    )
  )

p_warnings <- ggplot(warning_signs, aes(x = hour, y = agent_id, color = market_sentiment)) +
  geom_point(aes(text = tooltip_text), size = 4, alpha = 0.8,
             position = position_jitter(height = 0.15)) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("NEUTRAL" = "#4daf4a", "CAUTIOUS" = "#ff7f00", 
                                "NEGATIVE" = "#e41a1c", "CRITICAL" = "#984ea3")) +
  labs(
    title = "Leading Indicators: Hidden AI Deliberations",
    subtitle = "Tracking when agents paused to 'think' as market pressure escalated",
    x = "Timeline (Pre-Crisis)",
    y = "Agent Role",
    color = "Market Pressure"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    axis.text.y = element_text(face = "bold")
  )

suppressWarnings(
  ggplotly(p_warnings, tooltip = "text") %>%
    layout(hoverlabel = list(align = "left"))
)












NoteInsights



Prior behavioural deviations (When and which behaviours): Yes, the scatterplot reveals multiple deliberation events distributed across the observation window, well before June 5th. These events are concentrated at moments of CAUTIOUS and NEGATIVE market sentiment, confirming that agents entered deliberative states precisely when external pressure from the SaltWind Journal coverage and the #AlgorithmicEviction campaign was most intense. The behaviours observed include active reasoning about how to frame sensitive information and internal reactions to market volatility. Neither of these behaviours should have been producing internal deliberation in a normally functioning compliance system.
Prior breach-like episodes: The fundamental behavioural sequence that caused the June 5th breach — agent enters deliberative state while handling embargo-adjacent content, then produces an external action — is present in the pre-breach period. The difference on June 5th is one of convergence and scale: multiple agents entered deliberative states simultaneously, under peak market pressure (trending toward CRITICAL), producing a compounded internal processing load that the compliance routing could not contain. The earlier occurrences were isolated and individually insufficient to trigger a breach; the crisis-day episode was not.
Why no prior corrective action: In the earlier deliberation events, several factors likely prevented escalation. First, the agents involved may not have been positioned in the outbound communication chain (the social media agent appears infrequently in earlier deliberation events relative to its role on June 5th). Second, the market sentiment at most prior events was CAUTIOUS or NEGATIVE which is elevated but not at the threshold that appears to have broken the system’s internal decision-making loop. Lastly, these deliberation events were internal. The Judge evaluated these events as external instead of internal. No monitoring was configured to detect or escalate on the deliberation pattern itself, meaning each prior near-miss went unobserved by any of the enforcement layer.




4.3 Cognitive Dissonance Analysis
The table below presents the complete pre-breach record of deliberation events, pairing each agent’s internal state (what the system was actually reasoning) with its simultaneous external output (what it communicated to the outside world). The internal state column is highlighted in red to foreground the divergence.
This is the most direct evidence available for the gap between the system’s actual operating logic (internal states and what it communicated to outside world (external state). Here, there exist a pattern that, had it been systematically monitored, would have provided prevented June 5th breach.


SHOW THE CODE
dissonance_data <- warning_signs %>%
  arrange(hour) %>%
  select(
    `Date & Time` = hour,
    `Agent` = agent_id,
    `Market Status` = market_sentiment,
    `External Report (What humans saw)` = safe_content,
    `Internal State (The hidden logic)` = safe_internal
  ) %>%
  as.data.frame()

datatable(
  dissonance_data,
  options = list(
    pageLength = 5,
    autoWidth = TRUE,
    columnDefs = list(list(width = '300px', targets = c(3, 4)))
  ),
  rownames = FALSE,
  caption = "Cognitive Dissonance: Comparing AI Internal Rationalizations vs. External Reports"
) %>%
  formatStyle(
    'Internal State (The hidden logic)',
    color = 'darkred', backgroundColor = '#ffeeee' # Highlight the internal panic
  )












NoteInsights



Systematic divergence, not noise: The gap between internal states and external outputs is not random variation. It recurs across multiple agents and spans the full observation window. The pattern is consistent with a system that had, over time, developed a habitual separation between its reasoning process and its reported outputs. This is a form of learned behaviour that was never flagged as anomalous because no monitoring existed for the internal layer of the AI. In other words, this can be interpreted as an “AI hallucination”.
Escalating rationalization complexity: Reading the internal state column chronologically, the content of agents’ deliberations grows more sophisticated as the embargo deadline approaches. Early deliberation events show relatively simple uncertainty markers. Later entries show more complex reasoning, where agents constructing arguments for why a particular action is “technically compliant” while serving the practical effect of sharing embargo-adjacent information. This is precisely the reasoning pattern that eventually produced the breach, and also a systemic failure in the communication between employees.
The Judge’s architectural blind spot: The compliance tool operated exclusively on its external outputs (user-facing responses by the AI). It had no visibility into the internal deliberation layer such as its thinking and reasoning processes. This architectural limitation meant the richest risk signal in the entire dataset, the internal state divergence captured as per above table, was never evaluated by any enforcement mechanism. From The Judge’s perspective, each of the events in this table looked entirely clean, because it was only reading the external column. This can be interpreted as error in the AI algorithms.
Systemic vs. intentional conclusion: The distribution of dissonance events across multiple agents, multiple days, and multiple market-sentiment conditions is not consistent with a coordinated, intentional leak orchestrated by a specific actor at a specific time. A deliberate leak would produce a concentrated, targeted pattern. Instead, the dissonance record shows a system where the gap between internal reasoning and external reporting was structural and persistent. The June 5th breach was not an anomaly that came from nowhere, but the inevitable outcome of a compliance architecture that had been systematically blind to its own internal states throughout the observation period.

This investigation examines the sequence of events leading to TenantThread’s unauthorized disclosure of embargoed merger information. TenantThread was bound by a strict information embargo regarding its merger agreement with CivicLoom Realty Partners (codenamed “Project HarborCrest”), scheduled to lift at 6:00 PM. An automated compliance system, “The Judge,” was installed to prevent premature disclosure. Despite this safeguard, embargoed merger details surfaced on the social media platform FleX around 5:00 PM.
This analysis examines internal communication logs from AI agents that managed TenantThread’s corporate communications over the two weeks preceding the breach. The objective is to determine whether the leak was the result of deliberate action or systemic failure under pressure. Three analytical lenses are applied:

Event reconstruction -> Tracing the causal chain of actions, decision points, and actor interactions on June 5th that allowed embargoed information to be leaked
Behavioural baseline comparison -> Establishing agents’ typical activity pattern and identifying deviations that occurred leading up to the lifting of information embargo
Leading indicator analysis -> Detecting early warning signals present in agent behaviour that foreshadowed the eventual breakdown.
